::: {.module-line .content-visible when-format="html"}
**Module 4** · 50 min · [Open the slides for this module](04-physics-slides.html)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
- Give a game object a physics body.
- Use velocity, acceleration and drag to make movement feel right.
- Tell `collider` from `overlap`, and react to both.
- Use groups and the debug overlay.
:::

## Where you start

[Stopping point B](03-movement.qmd#what-you-have) moves the researcher by changing `x` and `y` by hand. That works until two things need to touch: walls, carts, a freezer you can't walk through. Checking every pair yourself gets out of hand fast.

**Arcade physics** does it for you. You give objects a **body**, tell Phaser which bodies affect each other, and it moves them and keeps them apart.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Phaser has two physics engines. **Arcade** uses only axis-aligned boxes and circles, and it's fast and predictable. That's what almost every 2D action game needs. **Matter** does real rigid-body physics: rotating shapes, stacking, joints, slopes. It's slower and much harder to control. *Cold Chain* and this course use Arcade. If you ever need things that tumble, look at Matter.
:::

## Turn physics on

In `src/main.js`, add a `physics` block to the config:

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopC/src/main.js" lines="14-17" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`default: 'arcade'` makes Arcade available as `this.physics` in every scene. The `debug` line turns the debug overlay on when the address ends in `?debug`, as in [lesson 0](00-engine.qmd#exercises). You'll use it constantly from now on.
:::

## Bodies and game objects

A game object is what you see. A body is what the physics engine sees: a box, its velocity, what it bumps into.

```js
// a sprite and its body, in one call
this.player = this.physics.add.sprite(100, 270, 'researcher', 1);

// or give a body to something you already made
this.physics.add.existing(this.freezer);
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The body is `sprite.body`. By default it's the size of the picture, which is often wrong: the researcher's picture includes empty space and a head. *Cold Chain* shrinks the body to the feet, so the researcher can walk "behind" the top edge of a bench:

```js
this.player.body.setSize(18, 14).setOffset(7, 17);
```

Turn on `?debug` and you'll see the body (a box), separate from the picture.
:::

## Velocity, not position

With a body, stop changing `x` and `y` yourself. Set **velocity** in pixels per second, and the physics engine moves the body every frame, using `delta` for you.

```js
this.player.setVelocity(dx * 200, dy * 200);   // no delta needed
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
You *can* still set `x` on an object with a body: the body copies its game object's position at the start of every physics step. But physics never sees that as movement. There's no velocity, so a big jump can skip straight through a wall, and anything it bumps into gets no push. Move bodies with velocity. To teleport one on purpose, use `body.reset(x, y)`, which moves it and zeroes its velocity.
:::

## Acceleration and drag

Setting velocity directly feels robotic: full speed instantly, stop instantly. Real things speed up and slow down.

```js
this.player.setMaxVelocity(220);                 // top speed
this.player.setDrag(1800);                       // slowing down when you let go
this.player.setAcceleration(dx * 1400, dy * 1400); // speeding up while a key is down
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- **Acceleration** changes velocity over time, in pixels per second per second.
- **Max velocity** caps it.
- **Drag** slows the body down, but only on an axis with **no acceleration**. That's why the researcher glides to a stop when you let go, and why drag doesn't fight you while you're walking.

These three numbers are most of what makes movement "feel" a certain way. High acceleration and drag: snappy and precise. Low: floaty, slippery, heavy. You'll tune them in exercise 4.4, and *Cold Chain* lowers the drag on spills to make them slippery.
:::

## A class for the player

The researcher has enough behaviour now to deserve its own class. It **extends** `Phaser.Physics.Arcade.Sprite`, so it's a sprite with a body that also knows how to walk.

```js
import Phaser from 'phaser';

export class Researcher extends Phaser.Physics.Arcade.Sprite {
  constructor(scene, x, y) {
    super(scene, x, y, 'researcher', 1);
    scene.add.existing(this);          // put it on screen
    scene.physics.add.existing(this);  // give it a body
    this.setCollideWorldBounds(true);  // replaces Clamp from lesson 3
    this.body.setSize(18, 14).setOffset(7, 17);
  }

  walk(direction) {
    this.setMaxVelocity(220);
    this.setDrag(1800);
    this.setAcceleration(direction.x * 1400, direction.y * 1400);
    if (direction.x !== 0) this.setFrame(9).setFlipX(direction.x < 0);
    else if (direction.y !== 0) this.setFrame(direction.y < 0 ? 5 : 1);
  }
}
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Put it in `src/objects/Researcher.js` and make one in `create()` with `this.player = new Researcher(this, 96, 272);`. `direction` is a `Phaser.Math.Vector2`: build it from the keys as in lesson 3, then call `.normalize()` instead of dividing by the length yourself.

The scene stays short, and everything about *how the researcher moves* lives in one file. Lesson 5 adds walking animations to `walk()`.
:::

## Static and dynamic

Walls never move. Give them **static** bodies: cheaper, and nothing can push them.

```js
this.walls = this.physics.add.staticGroup();
this.walls.create(16, 16, 'lab', 2);   // a wall tile
this.walls.create(48, 16, 'lab', 2);
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
A **group** is a collection of similar objects that share settings and can be collided with all at once. A static group makes static bodies.

Stopping point C builds a whole room of walls and benches from a list of strings, one character per tile. Lesson 6 replaces that with a map drawn in Tiled.

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopC/src/scenes/Play.js" lines="4-26" >}}

If you move or scale a static body after making it, call `refreshBody()`. Static bodies don't update themselves, which is what makes them cheap.
:::

## Collide or overlap

You tell Phaser which pairs of things interact, once, in `create()`.

```js
this.physics.add.collider(this.player, this.walls);   // solid: push apart
this.physics.add.overlap(this.player, this.sample, this.pickUp, null, this);  // just tell me
```

| | `collider` | `overlap` |
|---|---|---|
| Bodies are pushed apart | yes | no |
| Callback when they touch | optional | the whole point |
| Use for | walls, carts, the freezer | pickups, zones, triggers |

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Each takes two things (a sprite, a group, a tilemap layer), an optional callback, an optional **process callback** (return `false` from it to skip a collision), and the value of `this` inside the callbacks. That last argument is why there's a lone `this` at the end: without it, `this` inside `pickUp` would not be the scene ([lesson 1](01-javascript.qmd#the-one-thing-about-this)).

The callback gets the two objects that touched, in the same order you passed them.
:::

## Pick up, put down

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopC/src/scenes/Play.js" method="pickUp" >}}

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopC/src/scenes/Play.js" method="deliver" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`disableBody(true, true)` turns off the body **and** hides the picture, so the overlap can't fire again. `enableBody(...)` brings it back. This is how you reuse objects instead of destroying and recreating them. Ignore the `sound.play` lines for now: sound is lesson 5.

The **drop zone** is an invisible `zone` with a static body, a bit bigger than the freezer. The freezer itself is solid (a `collider`), so you can never overlap it; the zone in front of it is what you overlap.
:::

## Carts that bounce forever

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopC/src/scenes/Play.js" method="addCart" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- `setBounce(1)` keeps all the speed after hitting something, so a cart that hits a wall comes straight back.
- `setCollideWorldBounds(true)` makes the edges of the world solid.
- `setPushable(false)` means other bodies can't shove it. Without it, walking into a cart pushes it sideways out of its lane, and it keeps going that way (exercise 4.3).

Carts are a dynamic group (`this.physics.add.group()`), because they move.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Phaser 3 habit" .phaser3}
In Phaser 3, `group.children.each((cart) => ...)` loops over a group. In Phaser 4, `children` is a plain JavaScript `Set` with no `each`. Use `group.getChildren().forEach((cart) => ...)`.
:::

## Getting hit

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopC/src/scenes/Play.js" method="bump" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The collider separates the researcher and the cart; the callback adds a knockback. `player.x - cart.x` points from the cart to the player, so the researcher flies *away* from it. `normalize()` makes that length 1, and `scale(320)` makes it a speed.
:::

## See the bodies

Add `?debug` to the address.

{{< game stopping-points/stopC debug="true" caption="Stopping point C with ?debug. Pink boxes move, blue boxes are static, green lines show velocity." >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
When something collides wrongly (stuck on a corner, hit by thin air, walking through a wall), the debug overlay is the first thing to turn on. Nine times out of ten the body isn't where you thought.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 4.3: Spot the bug — the runaway cart" .exercise #ex-4.3}
In a labmate's game, walking into the side of a cart shoves it out of its lane, and it drifts off diagonally forever. Their `addCart` is below. What's missing?

```js
addCart(x, y, axis, speed) {
  const cart = this.carts.create(x, y, 'cart');
  cart.setBounce(1).setCollideWorldBounds(true);
  cart.setVelocity(axis === 'x' ? speed : 0, axis === 'y' ? speed : 0);
  return cart;
}
```

[Answer](../answers/04-physics-answers.qmd#ex-4.3)
:::

## Key points

- Arcade physics gives objects boxy **bodies** and moves them by velocity. Turn it on in the game config.
- Move bodies with velocity or acceleration, never by setting `x` and `y`. `delta` is handled for you.
- Acceleration, max velocity and drag decide how movement feels. Drag only acts when acceleration is zero.
- **Static** bodies (walls) never move. **Dynamic** bodies (players, carts) do. Groups hold many of either.
- `collider` pushes bodies apart; `overlap` only reports. Both take a callback and the value of `this`.
- `?debug` shows the bodies. Use it whenever collisions look wrong.
